items.title: Suicide Prevention and Awareness
items.author: Cpl Ella Cadby
items.summary: MARINE CORPS AIR STATION IWAKUNI, Japan – According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there are roughly 132 deaths per day by suicide in the United States. Suicide prevention is not the responsibility of one, but of all. It is a community effort built on those who recognize when someone may need support, knowing where the available resources are and being willing to connect people with them.
items.body: MARINE CORPS AIR STATION IWAKUNI, Japan – According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there are roughly 132 deaths per day by suicide in the United States. Suicide prevention is not the responsibility of one, but of all. It is a community effort built on those who recognize when someone may need support, knowing where the available resources are and being willing to connect people with them. There are many resources available across all military installations that can support service members facing mental, physical or spiritual challenges, including behavioral health personnel, the Chaplain, unit leadership, and other installation suicide-prevention programs. To maintain a healthy and ready force, it is imperative that all service members are not only aware of the various programs available but also understand they do not have to face difficult circumstances alone. It is common amongst service members to bear the weight of their hardships without reaching out for help from others. Independence and self-sufficiency are valuable qualities, however, in instances where the weight is too heavy to carry alone, seeking help can be an important step toward overcoming difficult trials. “Carrying an unbearable load in silence is not fortitude; it is a vulnerability,” said Chaplain Matthew Maestas with Marine Aircraft Group 12, 1st Marine Aircraft Wing. “True strength is having courage, humility, and self-awareness to admit when the pack is too heavy. Asking for assistance is not surrender; it is how we rearm and stay in the fight.” The slight, quiet changes in a person’s behavior often go unnoticed and yet, are sometimes among the first indicators that they’re struggling. Withdrawal, isolation, loss of interest and increased risk-taking are a few of many indicators that someone may need additional support. Recognizing those changes is the first step in getting someone the help they need. Marines wear two name tapes on their blouses. Their last name is written on the right and the one on the left says, “U.S. Marines.” Not just Marine, but “Marines.” It is our responsibility to check on the person sitting next to us, to have uncomfortable conversations with them, to listen without judgment and to be with them in crisis. “I believe community plays a huge part in suicide prevention,” said Lance Cpl. Johnathan Cabrera, an air traffic controller with Headquarters and Headquarters Squadron (H&HS), Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni. “Helping individuals build relations with not only others but with oneself gives people a sense of togetherness.” Recognize the signs, reach out and finally, connect people with the proper resources. The Chaplain, behavioral health, leadership and other installation resources “operate as an integrated network of support, each bringing distinct, complementary capabilities,” said Chaplain Maestas. -30-

items.title: Former ROTC commander turns B-52 static display into a classroom at Miramar Air Show
items.author: Kayla White
items.summary: Lt. Col. Nate Barnhart, 93rd Bomb Squadron commander, invited cadets from Air Force ROTC Detachment 060 at the University of Southern California, the detachment he previously commanded, to tour the aircraft and talk with its crew.
items.body: For three days, a B-52 Stratofortress from the 307th Bomb Wing drew crowds at the Miramar Air Show, the nation's largest military air show, Sept. 25-27, as aircrew from the 93rd Bomb Squadron spent hours at the static display answering questions from Southern California attendees. On the final day, the squadron's commander turned the bomber into a classroom for a group he knows well. Lt. Col. Nate Barnhart, 93rd BS commander, invited cadets from Air Force ROTC Detachment 060 at the University of Southern California, the detachment he previously commanded, to tour the aircraft and talk with its crew. "Although I will always have an affinity for Det 060 because of my time there, the experience gave me a sincere appreciation for teaching and working with cadets," Barnhart said. "It's different from aviators because you're really helping craft young people's lives and careers. And the ultimate reward is seeing them excel in their various careers on active duty." Teaching is central to Barnhart's current role. The 93rd BS leads the B-52 Formal Training Unit at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, where Reserve instructors work alongside active-duty 2nd Bomb Wing instructor pilots to train the aircrew who will fly the bomber for decades to come. For Barnhart, that mentorship starts well before anyone reaches the schoolhouse. "The key takeaway is understanding the importance of mentoring future officers before they even enter active duty," he said. "They rely on officers to give them their experience and current information. In turn, you can help in their decision making or, better yet, push certain ones to achieve more than they think they could." The cadets, who represent a range of career goals, came ready with questions. Cadet 3rd Class Katya Mendez, who graduates in 2029 and hopes to become a flight nurse, said the visit gave her insight she plans to bring back to campus. "I got to ask so many questions," Mendez said. "A lot of my job is to be an advocate to our leadership on behalf of my fellow cadets. It was cool to talk to Lieutenant Colonel Barnhart, getting to learn from him on how to improve [our] detachment." For Cadet 3rd Class Jessica Gonzalez, who aspires to be a fighter pilot, the biggest impression came from the people rather than the aircraft. "I loved hearing about aircrew culture and how they talk about it," Gonzalez said. "Their teammates are clearly a second family for them, and it's inspiring to see that they still love it after so long. It makes me believe that I could be that passionate about it, too." Cadet Capt. Tyler Jones, who also plans to pursue a pilot career, said the day renewed his sense of purpose. "It reignites passions for service and flying," Jones said. Lt. Col. Rene "Fez" Terriquez, who has commanded Det 060 since June 2025 and also serves as department head of Aerospace Studies at USC, said visits to operational units give cadets something the classroom can't. "Our goal is to connect what they're learning in AFROTC with the operational Air Force," Terriquez said. "Seeing a B-52 up close and talking to the people that fly and maintain them gives them a perspective that simply can't be replicated in the classroom." He said the value extends well beyond cadets headed for the cockpit. "Whether they want to be pilots, engineers, intelligence officers, nurses, or something else entirely, experiences like this help them see the bigger picture and understand how they can contribute to the mission," he said. "If they leave more motivated and excited about their future in the Air Force, then we've accomplished our goal." As the Air Force's only Reserve bomber wing, the 307th BW flies and maintains the B-52 at Barksdale and the B-1 at Dyess Air Force Base, Texas, holding both platforms to one standard. Events like the Miramar Air Show put that mission in front of audiences far from either base, and on the final day, in front of the officers who may one day carry it forward. "I'm really happy I came today," Jones said.

items.title: Hawaiʻi National Guard Sustains Dual-Island Recovery Operations, Prepares for Storm Nolo
items.author: Rachel Blaire
items.summary: The Hawaiʻi National Guard (HING) continues its active response across the state, balancing long-term recovery efforts on Hawaiʻi Island and Kauaʻi from back-to-back hurricanes while concurrently preparing for the potential impacts of Hurricane Nolo this weekend. Hurricane Nolo marks the fourth storm to threaten the island chain since August, highlighting an exceptionally intense period of tropical cyclonic activity in the region.
items.body:
The Hawaiʻi National Guard (HING) continues its active response across the state, balancing long-term recovery efforts on Hawaiʻi Island and Kauaʻi from back-to-back hurricanes while concurrently preparing for the potential impacts of Hurricane Nolo this weekend. Hurricane Nolo marks the fourth storm to threaten the island chain since August, highlighting an exceptionally intense period of tropical cyclonic activity in the region.

By utilizing an agile rotational force structure and drawing from a volunteer pool of approximately 5,500 personnel, the Guard remains fully postured to assist county, state, and community partners during this sustained multi-front response.

Following the widespread impacts of Hurricane Lala in August, which inundated Hawaii with 1.3 trillion gallons of water Aug. 14-16, 2026, the Guard mobilized Task Force Hawaiʻi to assist with extensive cleanup and humanitarian relief. In addition to physical clearance, Guard members, alongside the Hawaiʻi Fire Department and local emergency personnel, conducted 421 safety and wellness checks in remote areas such as the Kaʻū District.

“It definitely feels like an honor to help out the community and make things easier for them,” Spc. Brianna Diazescobar, 1st Squadron, 299th Cavalry Regiment said. “I know it's a very difficult time, so it just feels really good to help out, especially being here from the Big Island.”

To accelerate recovery efforts, HING partnered with the Pacific Air Forces to execute Operation Trek 808, rapidly airlifting electric restoration machinery from California to Hawaiʻi Island.

In one of the most culturally-sensitive operations, soldiers and airmen are assisting Hawaiʻi County and cultural practitioners with operations following severe landslides and flooding at Nāʻālehu Cemetery. They are removing debris from the cemetery and transporting human remains to be identified and recovered in partnership with the county.

“Our soldiers and airmen answered the call to service, putting community first in support of response and recovery efforts during Tropical Cyclone Lala,” said Hawaiʻi Adjutant General, Maj. Gen. Stephen Logan. “Their commitment to helping neighbors in need, from lifesaving rescues to damage assessments, reflect their dedication to help families begin to recover.”

Meanwhile, on Kauaʻi, where Hurricane Lowell unleashed destructive forces late on Sept. 7, 2026, Task Force Kauaʻi remains on the ground assisting with infrastructure and community stability.

Early in the response, HING deployed UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters from Oʻahu to transport 11 Transportation Security Administration (TSA) personnel to Līhuʻe Airport to facilitate the facility's rapid reopening. Aircrews also conducted aerial damage assessments alongside Kauaʻi Island Utility Cooperative (KIUC) officials to target power restoration efforts and scanned storm-swept terrain for distressed civilians.

Guard members are partnered with the Hawaiʻi Foodbank to distribute water, fresh produce and meals-ready-to-eat to residents facing storm-related grocery shortages.

"Most of my friends and family have been affected by the hurricane, and with the barge having delays and grocery stores not having food, it's really good to see everybody being helped," said Spc. Taylor Calixterio-Martinez, a Kauaʻi native assigned to Echo Company, 29th Brigade Support Battalion.

Even as recovery efforts are sustained across both islands, the HING is actively monitoring and staging assets in preparation for the potential effects of Hurricane Nolo. Leadership emphasizes that lessons learned from Lala and Lowell have refined the Guard's response tactics and inter-agency integration.

“This unprecedented storm season has tested our state, but it has also shown the strength of our joint partnerships,” said Maj. Gen. Stephen F. Logan, adjutant general of the Hawaiʻi National Guard. “Working hand-in-hand with county civil defense agencies, state leadership, FEMA, and our active-duty counterparts, we are ensuring that no island is left to recover alone. We will stand beside our communities through the healing of Lala and Lowell, and we are fully prepared to respond as Hurricane Nolo approaches."

items.title: Weapons Station Yorktown’s Youth Center Honors 9/11 Legacy with $2,500 Service Grant and First Responder Outreach
items.author: Max Lonzanida
items.summary: As part of a 9/11 service grant from the Boys & Girls Club of America, WPNSTA Yorktown's Youth Center visited with nearby first responders as a unique way community outreach opportunity.
items.body:
Story by Max Lonzanida Public Affairs Officer, Naval Weapons Station Yorktown

Yorktown, Va. (September 18, 2026) Military affiliated children from the Youth Center onboard Weapons Station Yorktown honored the national legacy of September 11, 2001, earlier this month in a meaningful and impactfully unique way. This was done via a generous Boys & Girls Club of America (BCBA) 9/11 Day Outreach Grant in the amount of $2,500, which in-turn allowed for special 9/11 programming and outreach for first responders in the community.

This initiative aligned with the broader National Day of Service associated with 9/11 events across U.S. Navy installations, bridging the generational gap for Yorktown’s military affiliated youths who were born long after the tragic events of that fateful day. While none of the children at the Youth Center today were alive during the attacks, the grant-funded programs provided them with a meaningful connection to American history, the spirit of civic duty, and the heroic sacrifices made by first responders and service members.

Historical accounts denote the U.S. Navy’s immediate, decisive response following the 2001 attacks. In the fragile hours after the crisis unfolded, the Navy mobilized rapidly to defend the homeland and spearhead relief operations. Deploying from nearby Norfolk, the aircraft carrier USS George Washington (CVN 73) rushed to the waters off New York City to establish air defense and surface security over Lower Manhattan. Simultaneously, the hospital ship USNS Comfort (T-AH 20) sailed to Manhattan's Pier 92, providing an essential afloat command node, medical sanctuary, hot meals, and crucial respite for thousands of exhausted police officers, firefighters, and relief workers tirelessly searching Ground Zero.

As part of the 9/11 grant, Youth Center staff members hosted educational sessions for children enrolled in Youth Center programs. Discussions centered around the tragic events of that fateful day and the significance of national unity. Youth Center enrollees also had several opportunities to create thank you cards for local first responders, which were incorporated into lunch totes filled with healthy shelf-stable snacks and refreshments that were packed for first responders. The healthy refreshments and lunch totes were purchased with grant funds from the BCBA; which was a first award of its kind for any U.S. Navy installation the region.

The impactful heartbeat of the project culminated with visits to first responders in York County. On September 4th, school age children from the Youth Center visited Newport News Police Headquarters to deliver the specially packed lunch totes and tour the facilities. This allowed a unique opportunity to learn about fields in law enforcement and see law enforcement operations up-close. Another visit to York County’s Fire Station #2 allowed for the same interactions. The impactful visits with the firefighters, law enforcement officers and emergency personnel also allowed children to connect the roles of their service member parents who stand on the front lines every day.

"Our youth program is dedicated to helping young people build character, develop leadership skills, and realize their full potential," said Jerry Graham, NWS Yorktown Youth Center Director. "This grant provided a wonderful opportunity for our military youth to connect with history, honor the legacy of 9/11 through direct action, and express their heartfelt gratitude to our local heroes."

Inspiring projects like these underscores how Weapons Station Yorktown’s Youth Center aligns directly with overarching Navy Child and Youth Programs (CYP) Fleet & Family Readiness goals. Overarching objectives of Navy CYP programs denote that robust, accessible, and high-quality childcare is an indispensable operational force multiplier. When service members know their children are thriving in safe, enriching environments, they can execute their defense mission with total focus and peace of mind. Steadfast and episodic partnerships with organizations like BGCA allow opportunities for NWS Yorktown Youth and Teen Programs continue to empower the next generation—building resilient leaders, fostering civic pride, and strengthening the foundation of our military community as a cornerstone of the many Quality of Life initiatives across the Navy’s shore enterprise.

For more information regarding Weapons Station Yorktown and Cheatham Annex Youth Programs offerings, upcoming events, or registration details, contact the Youth Center directly at (757) 887-4310 or visit the official website at https://www.navylifema.com/programs/0cd02c04-dcb6-4502-8574-55516cad29f3?utm_source=gemini.

items.title: JIATF-401 and NORAD / NORTHCOM Conclude Falcon Peak 26.2, Establish Enduring Counter-UAS Test Lanes
items.author: LTC Adam Scher
items.summary: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 concluded its operational experimentation exercise, Falcon Peak 26.2, at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground, advancing the evaluation of emerging counter-unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) alongside operational warfighters and interagency partners.
items.body: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 concluded its operational experimentation exercise, Falcon Peak 26.2, at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground, advancing the evaluation of emerging counter-unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) alongside operational warfighters and interagency partners. Conducted in direct support of U.S. Northern Command and Joint Task Force Southern Border, the exercise provided operational assessments of counter-UAS capabilities against evolving unmanned threats. The event also established enduring counter-UAS testing and evaluation lanes at Yuma Proving Ground to support continued collaboration between the Department of War, operational units and industry. "Countering the threat of drones is both a warfighting and a homeland defense imperative," said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401. "Unmanned threats will continue to evolve, which increases the risk at home. We conducted Falcon Peak to support Northern Command and Joint Task Force Southern Border, working directly with users in the field to ensure we understand their needs and deliver the best capability on the market." Throughout Falcon Peak 26.2, participating systems were evaluated against standardized Department of War test criteria. Performance data was consolidated into JIATF-401's centralized data repository to support rapid assessments and inform acquisition decisions. The dedicated counter-UAS testing and evaluation lanes established during Falcon Peak 26.2 will remain operational at Yuma Proving Ground. This testing capability will allow commercial developers and defense partners to continually evaluate and improve their systems. "One of the primary benefits of Yuma Proving Ground is its range instrumentation," said Ross. "Industry partners need to know the exact details of how their product performs. By establishing enduring counter-UAS test lanes here, industry does not have to wait for the next iteration of Falcon Peak to improve their systems. Companies can come directly to the range, receive immediate feedback, iterate on their systems, and rapidly deliver improved tools to our service members." Ross also emphasized the importance of interoperability and continued adaptation as the counter-UAS threat evolves. "There is no single solution or silver bullet to solve this problem,” said Ross. "Counter-UAS systems must function like Lego blocks. By standardizing common protocols and tactical interfaces, we are enabling vendors to plug their capabilities directly into our command-and-control networks. We don't just want to buy finished products. We want to build an enduring ecosystem of industry partners capable of continuous adaptation." To further connect industry, acquisition authorities, and operational units, JIATF-401 directs commercial developers, defense stakeholders, and warfighters to the Department's centralized counter-UAS marketplace at drones.mil. This platform provides a centralized resource for testing standards, commercial opportunities, and other information intended to connect developers with operational users. "Our goal is to ensure the limiting factor in defending our nation is never the equipment," said Ross. "By pairing persistent testing lanes at Yuma with the marketplace resources at drones.mil, we are building a continuous pipeline that moves verified, combat-effective C-UAS capabilities from the proving ground into the hands of warfighters at home and abroad."

items.title: UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: An air base in England used by American bombers to strike Iran was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27. The post UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
An air base in England where American bombers used to strike Iran are based was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27.

Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after being stopped close to RAF Fairford, police said, and explosive ordnance disposal technicians were dispatched to the scene. RAF Fairford is a British base currently hosting a dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which have been stationed there for around seven months for strikes on Iran.

President Donald Trump said the suspects were “looking to do big damage” to the U.S. at RAF Fairford and called the arrests “fantastic” before boarding Air Force One on Sept. 27.

“We had them under view for a long time and we got them,” Trump added. “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation.”

The base has been under increased security for days, which included the placement of vehicles around the perimeter, people familiar with the matter said. The threat level at the base was raised before the suspects were arrested. A U.S. Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss specific force protection measures, citing operational security.

Explosive ordnance teams from the British Army were called in to inspect the scene, and helicopter video footage aired by multiple U.K. news outlets showed a robot and personnel inspecting three white vans near the base fence, with B-1Bs parked on base nearby.

“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.

Police said they were called by a local after receiving a report about three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is located in Gloucestershire in southwest England.

“At around 12:45 a.m. today … police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be traveling towards the air base,” the Metropolitan Police, which investigates terrorism cases in the U.K., said in a Sept. 27 statement.

The U.K. government is still investigating the incident, counterterrorism officials said.

“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said. “As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”

RAF Fairford does not have permanent U.S. Air Force aircraft assigned there, but it has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.

“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our other U.K.-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people, and their families.”

Roadblocks, large machinery, and armed police have been seen around the base. Eighty-five homes in the nearby village of Whelford were evacuated.

“The emergency services have well-rehearsed plans for dealing with major incidents,” Gloucestershire Police assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said. “A cordon is in place as a precaution and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time.”

The B-1Bs at Fairford were heavily used during Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale air campaign against Iran in the spring, when the base housed some two dozen bombers including B-52 Stratofortresses.

Since a shaky ceasefire in April, most of the B-1Bs have remained while the U.S. carried out occasional strikes, including at least one involving a B-1 from Fairford. The bombers have regularly conducted training sorties out of the U.K.

The U.K. government gave permission for the base to be used in strikes on Iran in March under former Prime Minister Kier Starmer, for what the U.K. considers collective self-defense strikes. Burnham reaffirmed that decision in July, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned the U.K. government that it considered Fairford a legitimate target for attack. The U.K. government said in July it was prepared to use the British armed forces to defend the base.

The U.S. Air Force said it would continue to cooperate with the U.K. government to ensure the safety of its bases in Britain. Another U.K. base with U.S. aircraft is RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath is also used as a stopover location for fighters heading to the Middle East from the U.S.

“The safety and security of our Airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We remain in close coordination with our U.K. partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities.”

items.title: Terror suspects wanted to do ‘big damage’ to air base used by US, Trump says
items.author: Toby Shepheard, Reuters
items.summary: British police on Sunday arrested five men on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offenses near an air base that hosts U.S. Air Force personnel.
items.body:
British police on Sunday arrested five men near an air base used by U.S. forces on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offenses after a tip that three vans were heading to the military airfield, which has been used to strike Iran.

U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to do “big damage” and had been under investigation by British and U.S. authorities.

British counter terrorism detectives leading the investigation said police received a call about three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling towards RAF Fairford in the west of England in the early hours of Sunday.

Five men were arrested by armed officers and later held on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. Police said they believed the incident was now contained.

POLICE WORKING TO UNDERSTAND CIRCUMSTANCES

“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said in a statement.

“As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”

Police said a 400-meter cordon was in place around the base as the bomb disposal unit investigated the vans. Local residents in 85 homes in a nearby village were evacuated, and armed officers were patrolling the site.

The British government, which has given authorization to the U.S. to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, said Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being updated on the incident.

“I know today’s incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country,” Burnham wrote on X.

Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow U.S. bombers to fly from Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.

Police have not said who they believed was involved in Sunday’s alleged incident. An Iranian-linked motive is considered the most likely, a source familiar with the investigation said, while a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot are also being looked at.

“The arrest in the UK was fantastic,” Trump told reporters, saying it was “an amazing job.”

“We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our port and working with the British worked out great. ... We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” Trump added.

On Sunday morning the base was blocked by armed police while large machinery also prevented access. Reuters witnesses said security had been increased at other bases used by the U.S., with armored vehicles and soldiers at the gates of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in eastern England.

DECLARATION OF A MAJOR INCIDENT

“A cordon is in place as a precaution, and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time,” Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone told reporters.

The Daily Mail website carried a photograph of five men without shirts who it said had been arrested.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.

“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the spokesperson said.

“We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”

British ministers have also previously briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks.

Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations.

A British military air base in central England was broken into in June 2025 by the Palestine Action protest group, which has since been proscribed as a terrorist organization.

items.title: U.S., Indian Forces Fly, Fight Together in Combined Air Assault
items.author: MAJ Ian Roth
items.summary: AULI, India — U.S. and Indian Army forces executed a combined air assault Sept. 25, seizing two objectives during Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026 in a mission that integrated soldiers from both nations into the same maneuver formations.
items.body:
AULI, India — U.S. and Indian Army forces executed a combined air assault Sept. 25, seizing two objectives as a part of Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026 in a mission that integrated soldiers from both nations into the same maneuver formations.

The operation began with battalion scouts moving forward to conduct reconnaissance of the objective area, said Capt. Gaston Adam, deputy operations officer for 1st Mobile Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division. The lead company moved into assault positions and isolated and secured the first objective before a second company moved to isolate the second objective ahead of the air assault.

Soldiers then air assaulted by Indian Army Advanced Light Helicopter Mk III, also known as the Dhruv Mk III, onto a landing zone near the second objective before dismounting and moving into position. Indian Army soldiers conducted their own air assault shortly after, fast-roping from a helicopter to join the assaulting force and seize the objective alongside U.S. forces. Both objectives were fully secured before the combined force transitioned into a hasty defense.

Capt. Adam said the mission's success depended on close coordination between U.S. ground forces and Indian Army aviation the day before the operation. U.S. and Indian Army forces conducted an air mission coordination meeting between the aviation task force and the ground force task force, followed by cold load training and aircraft familiarization that allowed soldiers to practice safely entering and exiting the Dhruv Mk III ahead of the mission.

"The integration between the ground force and the aviation task force, particularly the pilots, is integral to an operation like this," Capt. Adam said. "You have to be able to look that pilot in the eye and trust they're going to get you there safely. It builds confidence in the soldiers that they're actually going to reach their objective and can focus on their mission."

Capt. Adam said the mission's task organization reflected the exercise's emphasis on interoperability between the two armies. The lead company, led by a U.S. company commander, included two U.S. Army platoons and one Indian Army platoon. The second company, also under U.S. command, was organized the same way. A separate Indian Army company serving as a decoy element during the operation included two Indian Army platoons and one U.S. Army platoon.

"It just goes to show that even though we're mixing our formations together, we can still work together and execute a good plan," Capt. Adam said.

Capt. Adam said the exercise's systems and checklists, understood across both armies, were essential to the operation's success.

"We have systems and checklists that we've codified as an Army and that our partners understand," Capt. Adam said. "As we follow those systems and build shared understanding across the force, it delivers a successful operation."

Sept. 25's mission marked the first of three repetitions planned during YA26, with additional air assaults scheduled for Sept. 26 and Sept. 27 under different task organizations. Capt. Adam said future repetitions may include an Indian Army company commander leading a mixed formation of U.S. and Indian Army platoons.

"It's been great working with the Indian Army," Capt. Adam said. "The planning has been great."

Yudh Abhyas 2026 is the 22nd iteration of the annual U.S. Army Pacific-sponsored bilateral exercise between the U.S. and Indian armies, designed to enhance bilateral readiness, cooperation and interoperability. The exercise is scheduled to conclude Sept. 27 with a formal closing ceremony.

Since 2004, Yudh Abhyas, a U.S. Army Pacific-sponsored bilateral exercise with the Indian Army, has enhanced combined interoperability and strengthened the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific.

items.title: Army Special Operations Soldier dies in training incident
items.author: Jacqueline Hill
items.summary: FORT BRAGG, N.C. – A U.S. Army Special Operations Soldier died on Sept. 22, 2026, from injuries sustained during a military airborne training event in Nevada. The soldier has been identified as Sgt. 1st Class Andrew Frakes, 34, of Savannah, Georgia.
items.body:
FORT BRAGG, N.C. – A U.S. Army Special Operations Soldier died on Sept. 22, 2026, from injuries sustained during a military airborne training event in Nevada.

The soldier has been identified as Sgt. 1st Class Andrew Frakes, 34, of Savannah, Georgia.

“Sgt. 1st Class Andrew Frakes represented the finest qualities of our nation’s special operations forces and performed at the highest echelons of our military,” said Lt. Gen. Lawrence “Gil” Ferguson, Commanding General, U.S. Army Special Operations Command. “The loss of such an exceptional warrior is felt deeply across the Special Operations community. Our deepest condolences, thoughts, and prayers are with his family, loved ones, and teammates during this difficult time.”

Frakes’ awards and decorations include the Joint Service Commendation Medal with combat “C” device (second award), the Army Commendation Medal (second award), the Army Commendation Medal with “C” device, the Joint Service Achievement Medal with “C” device, the Joint Meritorious Unit Award, the Meritorious Unit Commendation, the Army Good Conduct Medal (second award), the National Defense Service Ribbon, the Afghanistan Campaign Medal with one bronze service star, the Inherent Resolve Campaign Medal with two bronze service stars, the Global War on Terrorism Expeditionary Medal, the Global War on Terrorism Service Medal, the Armed Forces Service Medal, the Humanitarian Service Medal, the Noncommissioned Officer Professional Development Ribbon with numeral 3, the Army Service Ribbon, the Overseas Service Ribbon, the NATO Medal, the Ranger Tab, the Master Combat Infantryman Badge, the Combat Infantryman Badge, the Expert Infantry Badge, the Pathfinder Badge, the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, the Military Freefall Parachutist Badge, the Parachutist Badge, and the Air Assault Badge.

The incident is currently under investigation, and no further details are available.

Questions regarding this matter should be directed to the U.S. Army Special Operations Command Public Affairs Office at mailto:PAO-USASOC@socom.mil.

items.title: Serving Where Her Story Began: U.S. Navy Reserve Capt. Returns to the Philippines during Pacific Partnership 2026
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: TACLOBAN CITY, Philippines – U.S. Navy Reserve Capt. Shirlene Sulatan first learned about the Americans who served and died in the Philippines during World War II as a third grade student at her elementary school in the Philippines.
items.body:
“I can still see my face crying, ‘Who are these Americans?’” Sulatan said.

Sulatan, a lively fixture of Pacific Partnership 2026 (PP26)’s medical line of effort who is rarely seen without a smile, vividly recalls her teacher talking about how Americans and Filipinos helped each other to survive during the war, and being so struck that she even “went home and read about it more.”

Those stories have stayed with her in her journeys as a service member from Europe to Southeast Asia over the years. A Filipino American nurse practitioner and senior nurse executive assigned to Expeditionary Medical Facility (EMF) 150 - Alpha at Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, California, Sulatan has now dedicated 28 years of her life to military service.

During PP26, her medical expertise and personal connection to the Philippines allows her to support the mission while giving back to her native home.

“This is my fourth year participating in Pacific Partnership, but this is the first time I’ve been able to come back here,” said Sulatan. “To me, it means a lot because my roots are here. Even just hearing my dialect being spoken everywhere, I’m like, ‘Oh, OK, I’m really home.’ The food and just the warmth of the people, it means so much.”

Sulatan was born in 1969 in Malaybalay, Bukidnon, on the Philippine island of Mindanao. One of six children, she was raised by a mother who taught home economics and a father who worked in business.

“I remember we were very poor,” Sulatan reminisced. “I had to fetch water from the river, bring it back to the house and use it to wash the dishes. I even learned how to take a shower with just one gallon of water because I didn’t want to go back to the river to fetch more.”

Despite this, her parents were determined that their six children would pursue higher education. Her mother eventually went abroad to work as an au pair, sending all of her earnings back home so Sulatan and her five siblings could finish college.

“Our parents always told us every time we eat, no one is getting married in this family until you finish college,” said Sulatan. “So we knew that we had to go to college.”

Sulatan earned her nursing degree in the Philippines before moving to the United States in 1992 and beginning to build a life there with her husband. She joined the Navy Reserve in 1998 while working multiple jobs, raising a baby and continuing her education. After advancing to Hospital Corpsman 1st Class and earning her master’s degree as a family nurse practitioner, she commissioned through the Hospital Corpsman (HM) to Bachelors of Science in Nursing program, expanding the ways she could care for service members, veterans and communities around the world.

“I'm very thankful that my job is all about taking care of people, taking care of patients, young sailors and young officers, because I think it goes a long way,” said Sulatan. “If I had to do it all over again, I would still do it the same way.”

Today, Sulatan lives in Kona, Hawaii, and works for the Department of Veteran Affairs, where she cares for veterans, including those experiencing mental health challenges. In uniform, she continues to serve as a Navy Reserve nurse practitioner and senior medical leader. That path has now brought her back to the Philippines through Pacific Partnership.

“To me, Pacific Partnership means a lot because of the partnerships and the relationships we are establishing with people,” Sulatan said.

For Sulatan, building relationships as a U.S. service member with the local Filipino community is part of what makes humanitarian work and her military service meaningful.

“To me, doing humanitarian work is the best job in the military, because you’re really making an impact,” Sulatan said. “And getting to experience the culture of these people and meeting new people.”

Returning to the Philippines has given Sulatan a chance to share the wealth of medical knowledge she has gained since her career began in the Philippines. After earning her first master’s degree in 2007, she completed a doctorate and earned a certification as a nurse practitioner. She later earned a second master’s degree through the Naval War College, and her third master’s degree in public health from National University in San Diego.

“Coming here, I’m like, ‘Oh, I can finally serve my people too,’” Sulatan said.

She hopes the mental health knowledge she’s shared during Pacific Partnership will help local medical professionals continue caring for their communities after the mission ends.

“I hope they will continue to grow, that they will continue to be able to take care of their people, because their people are their best assets,” Sulatan said. “If you have a healthy nation physically, then you have a healthier economy because these people are able to work and serve as well.”

Sulatan continues to have that same drive to serve that she first felt as a third grader and says she does not plan to retire anytime soon. She plans to serve as long as the U.S. Navy will have her.

“Until they put me on a wheelchair and say, ma'am, you gotta go, you can't even do your squats anymore,” Sulatan exclaimed jokingly.

She plans to continue broadening her education and her service in the U.S. Navy. Most of all, she wants to share her knowledge and service with the communities the military has brought her to, particularly focusing on others mental health. For now, Pacific Partnership is one of the many ways she can share her vast experience, particularly in mental health.

“There is no limit to the possibilities on how to serve as well,” she said. “...because I know people who wake up every day and want to serve too… and I want to inspire them that service is really, you know, what makes our life more meaningful.”

Now in its 22nd iteration, the Pacific Partnership series is the largest annual multinational humanitarian assistance and disaster management preparedness mission conducted in the region. Pacific Partnership works collaboratively with host and partner nations to enhance regional interoperability and disaster response capabilities, increase security in the region, and foster new and enduring friendships in the Indo-Pacific.

For more information about Pacific Partnership visit www.facebook.com/pacificpartnership, www.instagram.com/pacific_partnership/ or https://www.dvidshub.net/feature/PacificPartnership .

items.title: To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region that spans all three commands. The agreement comes at an important moment in NORTHCOM's evolution, as its mission grows more complex. The post To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine</a
items.body:
U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region where all three commands converge, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

NORTHCOM’s Gen. Gregory M. Guillot, U.S. European Command’s Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, and U.S. Pacific Command’s Adm. Samuel Paparo will finalize the agreement, which aims to strengthen information sharing and ensure that adversaries cannot exploit the geographic boundaries among the commands.

U.S. Northern Command’s long-standing motto, “We have the watch,” has taken on greater urgency in recent years as the potential means to attack the U.S. Arctic region have grown. Today, the command’s geographic focus stretches across Canada, Greenland, and south to Mexico and parts of the Caribbean, and the potential dangers have expanded to include a range of emerging threats, from intelligence-gathering balloons to ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones.

Guillot, in a September interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, said the command has managed the growth well. “Over the last couple of years, we’ve received a few new missions with Greenland, the Southern Border, Golden Dome, and the counter-UAS mission, and we’ve been able to evolve and incorporate those into our daily homeland defense operations, I think, seamlessly,” said Guillot, whose responsibilities also include heading the binational U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command, known as NORAD.

“The command is growing as the number of threats and the number of avenues of approach that they can use to threaten us increase,” he added of NORTHCOM.

The Arctic’s strategic importance has grown as melting polar ice has opened up the region for greater commercial traffic and resource exploitation.

Russia, which owns more than half the Arctic coastline, has long projected its military might in the region.

More recently, China has sought to assert itself as an Arctic nation, not because it controls territory there but because of its value as a transit venue, shortening the trade routes between China and Europe. China operates research vessels there, including submersibles.

“They’re seeking to move themselves forward militarily and become global power projectors, not regional power projectors, and part of that will involve holding us at risk through the Arctic and ensuring that policy in the Arctic reflects their interests,” retired Gen. Glen D. VanHerck, Guillot’s predecessor at NORTHCOM and NORAD, said in an interview.

A joint China-Russia bomber patrol in the region, which took off in 2024 from a Russian base, demonstrated closer ties between the two and raised concerns across North America and Europe about their growing cooperation.

“When you see Russia and China cooperating militarily in the Arctic, with a greater capacity arguably than anywhere else on Earth, I think that should give some signals that we should be paying attention to what’s going on in the region,” said Iris Ferguson, who served as deputy assistant secretary of defense for Arctic and global resilience from 2022-2025.

Ferguson sees closing the gaps between U.S. military commands that converge in the Arctic region as essential to enhanced security.

“There are multiple seams in the Arctic for the United States,” she said. “The one between NORTHCOM and EUCOM is a significant one and is one area that deserves more attention.”

NORTHCOM led the drive to formalize an agreement with its fellow combatant commands, working closely with EUCOM and its boss, Grynkewich, who is also NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, with critical ties to NATO’s Nordic allies. Through NATO, Grynkewich is responsible for defending what NATO dubs the High North, comprising Canada, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, and the U.S. The alliance held multiple large-scale Arctic exercises this past summer, some of which Air & Space Forces Magazine experienced firsthand. NATO’s Arctic Sentry “enhanced vigilance activity” operates in cooperation with NORAD and NORTHCOM, and alliance officials describe that cooperation as at a level not seen in decades.

Guillot said the potential threats aren’t limited to America’s largest potential adversaries.

“I see the threat to our continent changing not just from Russia and China, but from multiple adversaries,” Guillot said. “The biggest change is that it’s from all avenues of approach instead of just from the north, and it’s with systems that could affect us from further away. So therefore our defense capabilities need to be expanded further from our borders to make sure that we’re defending at the appropriate range.”

“What that necessitates is cooperation with EUCOM, PACOM, and SOUTHCOM, where we can exchange information, pictures, intelligence, and even resources to defend further away,” Guillot said.

VanHerck applauded efforts to strengthen Arctic security and stop threats before they reach North America.

“Homeland defense doesn’t start in the homeland,” VanHerck said. “It starts forward with allies and partners and fellow combat commanders forward. Ideally, you have a posture and a presence and enough domain awareness that you deter those activities before they ever start. And if they’re going to attack, you can defeat those adversaries or capabilities further forward.”

The Trump administration has made Arctic security a centerpiece of its foreign policy, pressing to win new concessions for American basing in Greenland, expanding beyond a single Space Force installation to establish two new bases. Demonstrating the critical nature of Greenland to North American security, the administration transferred responsibility for Greenland, a territory of Denmark, to U.S. Northern Command, removing it from U.S. European Command’s area of responsibility.

That transfer is far from symbolic. “A lot of exercises and operations that we would normally conduct either unilaterally, or perhaps with Canada through NORAD, we’re now doing with other countries to include Denmark,” Guillot said.

A recent exercise with the U.S. and allied nations marked the first time Danish F-35s landed in Greenland.

U.S., Canadian, and Danish forces conducted joint Operation Arctic Vanguard and NATO exercises in Greenland this month that drew F-35As from continental U.S. bases, U.S. F-16s from Alaska, Canadian CF-18s, and Danish F-35As. French air-to-air refueling aircraft and NATO-operated E-3 AWACS command-and-control jets also joined the operations as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry.

Referencing the recent exercises, Guillot said allies were “fully integrated” and “operating in multiple lanes at the same time,” a shift from a few years ago when the U.S. may have conducted unilateral training instead. Operating as an integrated whole creates dilemmas for adversaries and acts as a force multiplier for the allies.

“That is possible due to the great relationship and partnering by the Danish forces,” Guillot said.

On the other side of North America, near Alaska, the U.S. and Canada recently conducted a joint exercise practicing striking maritime targets in the Bering Sea, using aircraft, surface vessels, and a submarine. The U.S. has also conducted joint naval operations with Canada that involve the U.S. Coast Guard alongside the U.S. military. Those exercises fall under Operation Tundra Merlin, which focuses on deterrence near Alaska, including the western Arctic and Northern Pacific. Pacific Air Forces aircraft stationed in Alaska also supported Arctic Vanguard on the other side of NORTHCOM’s region.

Alaska’s geographic size and placement at the nexus of the NORTHCOM and PACOM areas of responsibility places it in proximity to potential threats from China, Russia, and North Korea.

“I don’t think people appreciate the role that Alaska plays for our homeland defense mission, but also for our Indo-Pacific mission,” said Ferguson, who also served as a senior advisor to the Air Force on the Arctic. “Alaska is critical as a place of power projection to be able to project power not only into the Indo-Pacific in the event of a contingency, but also into the European theater.”

The exercises underscore Guillot’s broader Nordic Bridge initiative, launched earlier this year to better integrate allied operations across the Arctic. It includes coordination among the various U.S. combatant commands that touch on the region, as well as Canada, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland, all NATO allies. Working together, they aim to enhance domain awareness and interoperability.

“We’re working with other friendly Arctic nations to increase our presence,” Guillot said, “to increase and expand the deterrence, and make sure that every exercise we do up there is multinational and along multiple avenues of approach.”

items.title: "Tropic Lightning" Enables “Warrior” Brigade to Forge C2 Capabilities in the Dirt
items.author: CPT Eric-James Estrada

items.body:
SCHOFIELD BARRACKS, Hawaii – Leaning forward, his face smudged with camouflage paint, U.S. Army Maj. Nathan Sitterley analyzed the flow of data across his laptop screen. From inside a tactical operations center at East Range, the battalion executive officer for the 1st Battalion, 21st Infantry Regiment "Gimlets," tracked friendly forces and identified opposition forces on a large map display. For Sitterley and the Soldiers of the 2nd Mobile Brigade, this was where the Army’s ongoing operational evolution of its command-and-control systems met the friction of a live, tactical fight.

The exercise, known as Nakoa Fleek, served as the culminating training event for Lightning Surge 5, the 25th Infantry Division's multi-phase campaign to modernize its command-and-control architecture. While Lightning Surge focused on the strategic integration of new technologies, Nakoa Fleek was where these systems were employed in a tough, realistic environment, providing the opportunity to turn promising technology into a decisive combat capability.

"The controlled environment gets you to the 50-yard line," Sitterley said. "The last 50 yards happen out here, where you're battling latency, power, and connectivity issues right alongside the opposition force. This is where we forge a real combat capability."

The training was part of the division's ongoing campaign to support the Army’s scaling of converged and modernized command and control capabilities, improving decision speed and operational effectiveness under tough, realistic Pacific training conditions.

The exercise, which certified the Warrior Brigade ahead of future operations, was structured across three distinct battle periods. The first phase, which ran from Sept. 14-17, was dedicated to what planners’ call "enabling the fight." During this period, Soldiers, leaders, and industry partners worked through the process of integrating new communications gear, sensors, and command-and-control nodes.

The initial phase highlighted a fundamental lesson of modernization. What works perfectly in a lab environment must be validated in the dirt, with real Soldiers operating under tactical constraints. This focus on the "last tactical mile" of technology integration is where the most critical learning happens.

That learning was evident as the brigade moved into the second battle period from Sept. 18–21, which focused on the main defensive fight and tactical maneuver. With the network established, the focus shifted to action. On Sept. 23, the exercise culminated in an air assault designed to evaluate the brigade’s capacity to synchronize intricate operational elements under realistic conditions. For the Soldiers of the 1-27th and 1-35th Infantry Regiments, this was the moment when technology met tactics.

"The goal is to get the right data to the right leader at the right time," said Maj. Rebecca Borrebach, the division's lead data engineer. "We're validating our ability to push a common operating picture from the cloud to the tactical edge, even in a disconnected environment. It’s about giving the tactical units the situational awareness they need to make faster, better-informed decisions."

As the exercise transitioned into its final battle period, from Sept. 22-25, the focus shifted again, this time to the key lessons learned. A major takeaway has been the critical importance of the human dimension.

"The feedback from the field is clear: if a Soldier can't figure it out quickly under pressure, it's not a combat-effective tool,” said Maj. Jay Trexler, the division's innovation officer.

This iterative process of testing, getting feedback, and adapting is the central theme of the exercise and a core component of the Army's broader modernization strategy. It is not about a single, revolutionary piece of technology, but the steady evolution of people, processes, and systems to build a more effective and combat credible force.

"This is how we stay nested with the Army's strategic direction," said Col. Graham White, the 25th ID Deputy Commander of Operations. "By focusing on an operational approach of 'where we were, where we are, and what's still missing,' we ensure that we are not just testing equipment but are actively building the warfighting capabilities the Army and the Joint Force need to win in the Pacific."

As Nakoa Fleek concluded, the lessons learned from the Soldiers of the 2nd Mobile Brigade are already shaping the next chapter of the Army’s modernization effort. The campaign will continue during Lightning Surge 6, a larger and more complex evaluation set to take place during the upcoming Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center 27-01 rotation.

During that exercise, elements of the 3rd Mobile Brigade will join the effort, helping to refine an even more advanced suite of capabilities, including enhanced decision-support tools and smarter, more autonomous networks. It is a deliberate, iterative process, ensuring that every evolution of the technology is proven, practical, and provides a decisive advantage to the warfighter on the ground.

items.title: U.S., Indian armies complete bilateral live-fire exercise during Yudh Abhyas 2026
items.author: SSG Kalina Hyche
items.summary: U.S. and Indian Army forces conducted a joint firepower demonstration integrating artillery, aviation, air defense, counter-unmanned aircraft and surveillance capabilities during exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026 at Mahajan Field Firing Range, Rajasthan, India, Sept. 24, 2026. U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Lt. Gen. Vikrant Suresh Deshpande, general officer commanding, 10 Corps, joined senior military leaders and distinguished visitors in observing the demonstration, which incorporated U.S. and
items.body:
RAJASTHAN, India - U.S. and Indian Army forces completed a bilateral live-fire exercise integrating artillery, air defense, counter-unmanned aircraft systems and aviation capabilities during exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026 at Mahajan Field Firing Range, Rajasthan, India, Sept. 24, 2026.

The joint firepower demonstration marked a major training milestone following days of bilateral preparation across the training area. U.S. and Indian Army personnel brought together multiple weapons systems and capabilities during an event designed to demonstrate their ability to plan, coordinate and execute complex operations in a combined training environment.

U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Lt. Gen. Vikrant Suresh Deshpande, general officer commanding, 10 Corps, observed the demonstration alongside senior U.S. and Indian military leaders and distinguished visitors.

The demonstration incorporated the Indian Army’s Pinaka multi-barrel rocket launcher, M777 ultra-light howitzer, Dhanush artillery system, L70 air defense guns, Swathi weapon-locating radar and AH-64E Apache attack helicopters. U.S. Army capabilities included the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, or HIMARS, and the Mobile-Low, Slow, Small Unmanned Aircraft Integrated Defeat System, or M-LIDS.

Bringing the systems together represented the progression of bilateral training conducted throughout Yudh Abhyas. In the days leading up to the demonstration, U.S. and Indian Soldiers conducted system familiarization, rehearsals, live-fire training and professional exchanges focused on understanding how each force employs its equipment and executes its respective missions.

U.S. Soldiers trained alongside Indian Army artillery personnel on systems including the M777 and observed Indian Army L70 Bofors live-fire operations. Personnel from both armies also exchanged knowledge on aviation, targeting equipment and counter-unmanned aircraft capabilities before those individual training efforts were incorporated into the larger joint demonstration.

The live-fire event brought artillery, aviation, air defense, counter-unmanned aircraft and surveillance capabilities into a shared training environment. Coordinating those capabilities required personnel from both armies to apply the familiarity with systems, procedures and tactical approaches developed throughout the exercise.

M-LIDS provided a counter-unmanned aircraft capability during the demonstration, while artillery and rocket systems from both armies demonstrated complementary fires capabilities. Aviation and air defense assets further expanded the scope of the event, allowing participating forces to train across multiple operational functions during a single bilateral exercise.

The distinguished visitor even provided senior leaders an opportunity to observe the progression of training at Mahajan Field Firing Range, from initial system exchanges and rehearsals to the integration of multiple capabilities during the joint firepower demonstration.

The event also demonstrated the value of sustained bilateral training. Repeated interaction between U.S. and Indian Soldiers throughout Yudh Abhyas allowed participants to develop greater familiarity with each other’s equipment, procedures and approaches before executing the culminating live-fire training.

Yudh Abhyas is an annual bilateral exercise between the U.S. and Indian armies designed to improve readiness and interoperability through shared experience and realistic training. The exercise supports the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership and prepares both armies to operate together during crises, contingencies and humanitarian assistance and disaster response operations.

items.title: 8th TSC hosts Initial Exercise Sustainment Conference for Talisman Sabre 27
items.author: SGT Austin Riel
items.summary: FORT SHAFTER, Hawaii — The 8th Theater Sustainment Command hosts the Initial Exercise Sustainment Conference, a sustainment-focused planning conference in preparation of Talisman Sabre 2027 on Fort Shafter, Hawaii from Sept. 21-25, 2026.
items.body:
FORT SHAFTER, Hawaii — The 8th Theater Sustainment Command hosts the Initial Exercise Sustainment Conference, a sustainment-focused planning conference in preparation of Talisman Sabre 2027 on Fort Shafter, Hawaii from Sept. 21-25, 2026.

TS27 is a biennial-bilateral exercise between Australia and the United States, with multinational forces participating throughout Australia. The exercise integrates joint combat readiness, multi-domain operations, and interoperability among participating allies and partners, providing an environment to train and validate the ability to plan, synchronize, and execute combined joint operations.

“When you look across the exercise campaign plan, this one sits …one of the signature keystone events where you have a significant amount of combat power and command and control within a very important piece of geography,” said Maj. Gen. Frederick Crist, commanding general of the 8th Theater Sustainment Command.

TS27 is an operationally focused, purpose-built field training exercise that demonstrates the ability of allies and partners to generate and employ a combined joint force in support of collective security throughout the Indo-Pacific region. The exercise planning framework is designed to enhance operational-level coherence across tactical activities and ensure alignment of tactical actions with operational objectives.

TS27’s framework emphasizes multinational participation and multi-domain integration across land, maritime, air, space, and cyberspace. These efforts are intended to strengthen shared messaging, operational posture, interoperability, and combined joint warfighting capabilities.

“It’s all about being able to bring incredible combat capability, exercising with the intention of getting better and building readiness, getting closer with interoperability a little bit more,” said Crist. “And at the end of the day, having a capability that has a deterrent effect.”

This year marks the 13th iteration of Talisman Sabre with a focus on Anti-Submarine Warfare Operations, Air Combat Operations and Long Range Logistics, Combined Joint Forcible Entry Operations and Non-Kinetic Operations.

Planners from 8th TSC, Australian Defense Forces, and U.S. military service members worked together during this time to plan and refine the logistics of TS27. While normally geographically dispersed, this opportunity provides the atmosphere for interoperability between the ADF and U.S. military forces.

items.title: USS Lake Erie, crew honored at decommissioning ceremony
items.author: LT Jamie Miller
items.summary: NAVAL BASE SAN DIEGO—Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruiser USS Lake Erie (CG 70) and the crews who have manned it, were recognized during a decommissioning ceremony, celebrating 33 years of faithful service, held at Naval Base San Diego, Sept. 25.
items.body:
NAVAL BASE SAN DIEGO—Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruiser USS Lake Erie (CG 70) and the crews who have manned it, were recognized during a decommissioning ceremony, celebrating 33 years of faithful service, held at Naval Base San Diego, Sept. 25.

During the ceremony, Capt. Drew Borovies, Lake Erie’s final commanding officer, reflected on the occasion. “Today, we gather not simply to mark the end of a ship’s active service, but to honor the generations of Sailors who have served aboard Lake Erie, the families who have supported them and the many commands, communities and friends who have stood alongside the ship throughout her distinguished career,” said Borovies.

Named after the United States Navy’s decisive victory in the Battle of Lake Erie during the War of 1812, Lake Erie was built by Bath Iron Works in Bath, Maine and christened by Mrs. Margaret Meyer, wife of Rear Admiral Wayne E. Meyer, on July 13, 1991. The ship commissioned on July 24, 1993, at Pearl Harbor Naval Station.

The decommissioning of Lake Erie is preceded by a legacy of firsts. The ship played a leading role in the development and operational testing of the Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense system, including several first-of-its-kind intercepts of ballistic missiles.

Lake Erie deployed to multiple regions including the Pacific, Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, Indian Ocean and the Caribbean, participating in numerous exercises and operations. The ship supported Operation Southern Watch in 1995 in addition to the withdrawal of peacekeepers in Somalia during Operation United Shield that same year. In February 2008, Lake Erie intercepted and destroyed a 5,000-pound errant U.S. satellite in Operation Burnt Frost. In 2017, the ship participated in Operation Inherent Resolve conducting escorts through the Strait of Hormuz and deployed to Sri Lanka to provide lifesaving humanitarian assistance after severe flooding and landslides devastated many regions of the country and left 10,000 displaced.

The ship concluded its service to the nation in June after 11 months of sustained operations at sea to the U.S. 4th Fleet area of operations in support of U.S. Southern Command-led Operation Southern Spear countering illicit maritime activity.

Guest of honor, Retired Rear Adm. Randall Hendrickson, presented the crew with the Battle “E” award and wished them farewell.

“You inherited this ship and added to the legacy habitually while you stood the watch,” said Hendrickson. “For that, the nation, the American people are grateful.”

“Our ship may be leaving the fleet, but her Sailors are not,” said Borovies. “They will take a piece of Lake Erie with them to their next commands, and in doing so, they will carry this ship’s legacy forward.”

The inactivation, retirement and disposition of Lake Erie at the end of its lifecycle is in alignment with the Department of War initiative to invest in more modern warfare capabilities to ensure the United States’ competitive edge. Several other Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruisers remain in service as a key part of the Navy Surface Force. These ships are multi-mission surface combatants capable of supporting carrier strike groups, amphibious forces or operating independently.

For more news from Commander, Naval Surface Force, U.S. Pacific, visit http://www.surfpac.navy.mil/ or follow on Facebook at http://www.facebook.com/surfacewarriors and on Instagram at http://www.instagram.com/surface_warriors.
